narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 56.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction toward failure. Being in the second decile means you placed in the bottom 20% of your class that year, noticeably lower than the average of roughly the sixth decile among students who were accepted. This signal of recent academic performance weighed heavily against your application.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 3.30 it sits slightly above the 3.23 average of accepted students, which helped pull the prediction back toward passing. However, this positive effect was not strong enough to overcome the other factors.

Your family’s upper-middle income bracket also nudged the outcome toward failure, though less dramatically. While this bracket is the most common one among accepted students, the model still interpreted it as a mild risk factor in your overall profile.

Taken together, the model concluded your recent academic standing created too high a risk of bar exam failure for the program to admit you. To improve your chances next time, focus on raising your class rank in future years and consider retaking the LSAT if possible, as a stronger score could offset some of the earlier academic signals.
